## The Problem

R and C++ leave a function differently:

- A C++ exception walks back through C++ code and runs destructors.
- An R error jumps directly back to R. C++ destructors in its path do not run.

An R error is always possible when calling R. Allocation can fail, an interrupt
can arrive, and a warning becomes an error under `options(warn = 2)`.

At the interface between packages, `charport` therefore normalizes on R's
`Rf_error()`/long-jump system. This is the one error system every R package
shares, without requiring Rcpp, cpp11, or another C++ framework.

Inside C++ code, `charport` temporarily turns that R jump into a C++ exception.
Destructors run, and the original R error then continues. Rcpp and cpp11
perform this bridge differently, which is why `charport` selects a
compile-time adapter for each entry style.

The reverse direction is simpler: a C++ exception must not leave through a C
entry point. The outer boundary lets C++ cleanup finish before reporting an R
error on the main thread.

## Choose the Entry Style

| R enters through | Include order | Outer error boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Hand-written `.Call` | `charport.h` | `charport::r_boundary()` |
| Rcpp generated wrapper | `Rcpp.h`, then `charport.h` | Generated by Rcpp |
| cpp11 generated wrapper | `cpp11.hpp`, then `charport.h` | Generated by cpp11 |

Reader construction and Builder wrapping use the selected adapter internally.
Their ordinary use is the same in all three cases:

``` cpp
charport::Reader input(x);
charport::charvec::Builder output(input.size());

for(R_xlen_t i = 0; i < input.size(); ++i) {
  output.set(i, input[i]);
}

return output.to_sexp();
```

### Hand-Written `.Call`

A hand-written entry point supplies its own outer boundary:

``` cpp
#include "charport.h"

extern "C" SEXP C_copy(SEXP x) {
  return charport::r_boundary("copy", [&]() -> SEXP {
    charport::Reader input(x);
    charport::charvec::Builder output(input.size());
    for(R_xlen_t i = 0; i < input.size(); ++i) {
      output.set(i, input[i]);
    }
    return output.to_sexp();
  });
}
```

Place the boundary before any C++ objects whose cleanup matters. For an
additional raw R call, protect only that call:

``` cpp
return charport::unwind_protect([&]() -> SEXP {
  return Rf_eval(expression, environment);
});
```

A hand-written boundary also works in a file that includes Rcpp or cpp11:
`r_boundary()` recognizes the framework's unwind exception and continues the
original R error.

### Rcpp and cpp11

Include the framework normally, followed by `charport.h`:

``` cpp
#include <Rcpp.h> // or <cpp11.hpp>
#include "charport.h"
```

The include order lets `charport.h` select the matching adapter. You do not need
an additional `r_boundary()` because the generated wrapper already supplies
the outer boundary. `charport::unwind_protect()` uses the selected framework.

### Foreign Error-Handler Macros

A package that already has its own error-handler macro system can integrate
charport's standalone backend at that boundary. Catch `charport::r_unwind`,
record its token, and leave the catch block before continuing the R unwind:

``` cpp
SEXP unwind_token = R_NilValue;
try {
  charport::Reader input(x);
  // ...
} catch(const charport::r_unwind& error) {
  cleanup();
  unwind_token = error.token;
}

if(unwind_token != R_NilValue) {
  charport::continue_r_unwind(unwind_token);
}
```

Do not call `R_ContinueUnwind()` or otherwise long-jump from inside the live
catch block: doing so skips destruction of the in-flight C++ exception object.
The standalone token is preserved separately for each throw, and
`continue_r_unwind()` releases it before resuming the original R condition.

## Keep Protected Calls Narrow

Keep C++ objects that need reliable destruction outside the protected
callback:

``` cpp
Resource resource;

charport::unwind_protect([&]() -> SEXP {
  return one_R_call();
});
```

Avoid constructing such an object inside the callback before calling R. An R
error would jump over its destructor before becoming a C++ exception.

Charport's callback trampoline catches ordinary C++ exceptions and rethrows
them after returning through R's C code. This avoids sending a C++ exception
through C. It cannot recover a destructor that an R jump has already skipped.

## Provider Initialization

`init(SEXP)` may return `NULL` to decline a vector. Its error convention is
`Rf_error()` only; any possible C++ exceptions are caught within the callback.

If initialization needs both R-facing work and C++ state, do the R work first.
Once C++ state exists, an R error would jump over its destructors.

Range and indexed callbacks must not call R or throw. Release callbacks have no
error channel.

## Worker Threads

R calls and R errors stay on the main thread. Workers may do C++ work and report
C++ exceptions. A typical error path catches the worker exception, joins every
worker, and rethrows on the main thread. The outer boundary then reports it to
R after cleanup.

## Cost

There is no protection around Reader range access, indexed access, scalar
access, or worker loops. The fixed-cost bridge is used for Reader initialization,
final Builder wrapping, and explicit calls to `charport::unwind_protect()`.
